reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
clinicalPearls: Caused by deficiency of succinyl-CoA:glutarate-CoA transferase (SUGCT, encoded by C7orf10), an enzyme that activates glutarate to glutaryl-CoA, much of it in relation to intestinal/microbial-derived glutarate
Widely regarded as a benign biochemical trait, being one of the more common incidental findings of isolated glutaric aciduria on urine organic acid analysis
The biochemical signature is persistent isolated glutaric acid excretion in the urine without the neurological or metabolic features of glutaric aciduria type I
Crucially distinguished from glutaric aciduria type I (glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency), which causes an encephalopathic crisis and striatal injury and is a treatable serious disorder
It is also distinct from glutaric aciduria type II (multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency), which produces a broader acylcarnitine and organic acid disturbance
No specific treatment is required, and the main clinical importance is avoiding misdiagnosis as the more serious types
Inheritance is autosomal recessive; affected individuals are generally healthy
British spelling and paediatric context apply
reference.pathophysiology: SUGCT (succinyl-CoA:glutarate-CoA transferase) transfers coenzyme A from succinyl-CoA to glutarate to form glutaryl-CoA, a step important for handling glutarate, much of which derives from dietary and gut-bacterial sources. When this enzyme is deficient, glutarate is not efficiently activated and is excreted in the urine as isolated glutaric acid. Because this reaction is peripheral to the main lysine/tryptophan degradation route affected in glutaric aciduria type I, its loss does not cause accumulation of neurotoxic metabolites such as 3-hydroxyglutaric acid, and the condition remains clinically benign. The finding therefore reflects altered glutarate handling rather than a harmful metabolic block.
additionalDifferentials: Glutaric aciduria type I (glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency) with encephalopathy and striatal injury
Glutaric aciduria type II (multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency)
Secondary glutaric acid excretion from diet or gut flora
Other benign organic acidurias detected incidentally
Ketosis or fasting artefacts on organic acid analysis
additionalInvestigations: Urine organic acids showing isolated glutaric acid without 3-hydroxyglutaric acid
Plasma acylcarnitine profile (notably glutarylcarnitine) to distinguish type I and type II
Assessment for the neurological features and imaging changes of type I if in doubt
Molecular analysis of the SUGCT (C7orf10) gene
Repeat testing to confirm the persistent isolated pattern
Clinical review to confirm the absence of encephalopathic features
redFlags: Any encephalopathic crisis, macrocephaly, or movement disorder, which would point to type I rather than the benign type 3
Raised 3-hydroxyglutaric acid or glutarylcarnitine suggesting a pathogenic glutaric aciduria
Metabolic decompensation, which is not a feature of type 3
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent, as glutaric aciduria type 3 is a benign biochemical trait with no established associated disease and no need for treatment.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing benign type 3 as the serious, treatable type I
Failing to check 3-hydroxyglutaric acid and acylcarnitines to make the distinction
Instituting unnecessary dietary restriction or emergency protocols
Attributing unrelated symptoms to the incidental biochemical finding
references: Nyhan, Atlas of Inherited Metabolic Diseases
